There are also a small number of disyllabic words and an even rarer number of trisyllabic and polysyllabic words. ... A monosyllabic word is a word with only one syllable. The strong stress usually occurs on that syllable. Its structure is ['s]. [p.47] This sub-type is composed of a presyllable which has an unstress followed by a major syllable. The strong stress is on the last syllable. Its structure is [u.'s]. new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress (final) is exactly what the thesis describes for the Huay Salop dialect: strong stress on the last syllable of every 1-3 syllable word; refines with the secondary-stress/presyllable detail and the non-phonemic status.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress is non-phonemic and fully predictable: it falls on the major syllable, which is the only syllable of a monosyllable and always the last syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic phonological word (structures ['s], [u.'s], [,w.'s], [u.u.'s], [u.,w.'s], [,w.u.'s], [,w.,w.'s]). Stress is defined by intensity and vowel duration; tone (four tonemes) is the contrastive suprasegmental.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weak (secondary) stress falls on any minor syllable (a full C(C)V(C)+tone syllable in non-final position); zero stress on the presyllable /Cə/. Both occur only in non-final positions (p. 69 'It occurs on any minor syllable'; p. 71 minor syllable 'always takes a secondary stress'; presyllable 'always takes a zero stress').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says stress needs no marking in phonemic transcription because it is entirely predictable from position and syllable type. Words of 4-5 syllables are analysed as compounds or polysyllabic words with the same final-major-syllable pattern (p. 49-50).
new_statements.identity_note: Thanamteun (2000) describes the Pa-O (Taungthu) dialect of Ban Huay Salop, Tambon Huay Pha, Muang District, Mae Hong Son Province, Thailand (Northern Karen, Pa-O; ISO 639-3 blk), based on fieldwork with Thai-resident Pa-O speakers. It also summarises Jones (1961) on Taungthu in its literature review (pp. 18-19, PDF 31-32), which mentions stressed/unstressed allophones of tones and vowels but does not state a placement rule. The catalog entry is for Pa-O as a whole.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every sentence of the deciding quotation is on the cited pages of the scan we hold; I verified thesis pp.68 and 70 against rendered page images and pp.46-48 against the held scanned, locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 154-page 2000 Mahidol MA phonology thesis devoted to this language, which a 2015 Pa-O specialist (Jitwiriyanont, MANUSYA 18.2:72) identifies as the only phonological study of Pa-O outside Proto-Karen comparative work; Glottolog's descriptive list has nothing ranked above it (the other 'phonology' item, Nishida 1966/67, is a 19-page sketch of Southern Pa-O that I downloaded and found silent on stress, though its CV'CVC word canon matches the [u.'s] presyllable pattern). The two open items downloaded now (Jitwiriyanont 2015 acoustic tone paper; Nishida 1967) are both silent on stress and neither contradicts final prominence. sources.quote: No stress statement. Instrumental F0 study of 6 lexical tones (4 non-checked, 2 checked) of Southern (Thaton) Pa-O on 18 monosyllabic test words; phonological sketch gives 20 consonants, 11 vowels, 6 tones, no vowel-length contrast. Literature review p.72: 'There are a few linguistic studies on N. Pa-O (Jones, 1961; Burling, 1969; Thanamteun, 2000) ... Except for Thanamteun's study of N. Pa-O phonology, all studied Pa-O as part of Proto-Karen reconstruction.' Footnotes 1/3 identify the author's Chulalongkorn PhD on 'citation tones and tonal coarticulation in Pa-O continuous speech'.

sources.quote: No stress/accent statement (no occurrence of 強勢/アクセント/stress in the text). Describes Southern Pa-O (Pa'an) morphemes as monosyllabic CVC or disyllabic CV'CVC with a reduced glottal-checked first syllable (ka'tu 'head', ta'ka 'door', pa'li 'boat'), 4 tonemes (6 phonetic tone shapes), i.e. the same presyllable + full final syllable (sesquisyllabic) word shape that Thanamteun analyses as [u.'s]; consistent with, but not a statement of, final prominence.
